{{Short description|One of Fredholm's theorems in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Fredholm alternative''', named after [[Ivar Fredholm]], is one of [[Fredholm's theorem]]s and is a result in [[Fredholm theory]]. It may be expressed in several ways, as a theorem of [[linear algebra]], a theorem of [[integral equation]]s, or as a theorem on [[Fredholm operator]]s. Part of the result states that a non-zero complex number in the [[spectrum (functional analysis)|spectrum]] of a [[compact operator]] is an eigenvalue.

==Linear algebra==
If <math>V</math> is a <math>n</math>-dimensional [[vector space]], with <math>n</math> finite, and <math>T:V\to V</math> is a [[linear transformation]], then exactly one of the following holds:

#For each vector <math>v</math> in <math>V</math> there is a vector <math>u</math> in <math>V</math> so that <math>T(u) = v</math>. In other words: <math>T</math> is surjective (and so also bijective, since <math>V</math> is finite-dimensional).
#<math>\dim(\ker(T)) > 0.</math>

A more elementary formulation, in terms of matrices, is as follows. Given an <math>m \times n</math> matrix <math>A</math> and a <math>m \times 1</math> column vector <math>\mathbf{b}</math>, exactly one of the following must hold:

#''Either:'' <math>A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}</math> has a solution <math>\mathbf{x}</math>
#''Or:'' <math>A^T \mathbf{y} = 0</math> has a solution <math>\mathbf{y}</math> with <math>\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{b} \neq 0</math>.

In other words, <math>A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}</math> has a solution <math> (\mathbf{b} \in \operatorname{Im}(A)) </math> if and only if for any <math>\mathbf{y}</math> such that <math>A^T \mathbf{y} = 0</math>, it follows that <math>\mathbf{y}^T\mathbf{b} = 0</math> <math> (i.e., \mathbf{b} \in \ker(A^T)^{\bot}) </math>.
==Integral equations==
Let <math>K(x,y)</math> be an [[integral kernel]], and consider the [[System of linear equations#Homogeneous systems|homogeneous equation]], the [[Fredholm integral equation]],

:<math>\lambda \varphi(x)- \int_a^b K(x,y) \varphi(y) \,dy = 0</math>

and the inhomogeneous equation

:<math>\lambda \varphi(x) - \int_a^b K(x,y) \varphi(y) \,dy = f(x).</math>

The Fredholm alternative is the statement that, for every non-zero fixed [[complex number]] <math>\lambda \in \mathbb{C},</math> either the first equation has a non-trivial solution, or the second equation has a solution for all <math>f(x)</math>.

A sufficient condition for this statement to be true is for <math>K(x,y)</math> to be [[square integrable]] on the rectangle <math>[a,b]\times[a,b]</math> (where ''a'' and/or ''b'' may be minus or plus infinity). The integral operator defined by such a ''K'' is called a [[Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator]].

== Functional analysis  ==

Results about [[Fredholm operator|Fredholm operators]] generalize these results to complete normed vector spaces of infinite dimensions; that is, [[Banach space]]s.

The integral equation can be reformulated in terms of operator notation as follows. Write (somewhat informally)
<math display=block>T = \lambda - K</math>
to mean
<math display=block>T(x,y) = \lambda\; \delta(x-y) - K(x,y)</math>
with <math>\delta(x-y)</math> the [[Dirac delta function]], considered as a [[Distribution (mathematics)|distribution]], or [[generalized function]], in two variables. 
Then by [[convolution]], <math>T</math> induces a [[linear operator]] acting on a Banach space <math>V</math> of functions <math>\varphi(x)</math>
<math display=block>V \to V</math>
given by
<math display=block>\varphi \mapsto \psi</math>
with <math>\psi</math> given by
<math display=block>\psi(x)=\int_a^b T(x,y) \varphi(y) \,dy = \lambda\;\varphi(x) - \int_a^b K(x,y) \varphi(y) \,dy.</math>

In this language, the Fredholm alternative for integral equations is seen to be analogous to the Fredholm alternative for finite-dimensional linear algebra.

The operator <math>K</math> given by convolution with an <math>L^2</math> kernel, as above, is known as a  [[Hilbert–Schmidt integral operator]].
Such operators are always [[compact operator|compact]]. More generally, the Fredholm alternative is valid when <math>K</math> is any compact operator. The Fredholm alternative may be restated in the following form: a nonzero <math>\lambda</math> either is an [[eigenvalue]] of <math>K,</math> or lies in the domain of the [[resolvent formalism|resolvent]]
<math display=block>R(\lambda; K) = (K-\lambda \operatorname{Id})^{-1}.</math>

== Elliptic partial differential equations ==

The Fredholm alternative can be applied to solving linear [[elliptic partial differential equations|elliptic boundary value problems]]. The basic result is: if the equation and the appropriate Banach spaces have been set up correctly, then either

:(1) The homogeneous equation has a nontrivial solution, or

:(2) The inhomogeneous equation can be solved uniquely for each choice of data.

The argument goes as follows. A typical simple-to-understand [[elliptic operator]] <math>L</math> would be the Laplacian plus some lower order terms. Combined with suitable boundary conditions and expressed on a suitable Banach space <math>X</math> (which encodes both the boundary conditions and the desired regularity of the solution), <math>L</math> becomes an unbounded operator from <math>X</math> to itself, and one attempts to solve

:<math>L u = f,\qquad u\in \operatorname{dom}(L) \subseteq X, </math>

where <math>f \in X</math> is some function serving as data for which we want a solution. The Fredholm alternative, together with the theory of elliptic equations, will enable us to organize the solutions of this equation.

A concrete example would be an elliptic [[boundary-value problem]] like

:<math>(*)\qquad Lu := -\Delta u + h(x) u = f\qquad \text{in }\Omega,</math>

supplemented with the boundary condition

:<math> (**) \qquad u = 0 \qquad \text{on } \partial\Omega,</math>

where <math>\Omega \subseteq \mathbf{R}^n</math> is a bounded open set with smooth boundary and <math>h</math> is a fixed coefficient function (a potential, in the case of a Schrödinger operator). The function <math>f \in X</math> is the variable data for which we wish to solve the equation. Here one would take <math>X</math> to be the space <math>L^2(\Omega)</math> of all [[square-integrable function]]s on <math>\Omega</math>, and <math>\operatorname{dom}(L)</math> is then the [[Sobolev space]] <math>W^{2,2}(\Omega) \cap W_0^{1,2}(\Omega)</math>, which amounts to the set of all square-integrable functions on <math>\Omega</math> whose [[weak derivative|weak]] first and second derivatives exist and are square-integrable, and which satisfy a zero boundary condition on <math>\partial\Omega</math>.

If <math>X</math> has been selected correctly (as it has in this example), then for <math>\mu_0 \gg 0</math> the operator <math>L + \mu_0</math> is [[positive operator|positive]], and then employing [[elliptic estimates]], one can prove that <math>L + \mu_0 : \operatorname{dom}(L) \to X</math> is a bijection, and its inverse is a compact, everywhere-defined operator <math>K</math> from <math>X</math> to <math>X</math>, with image equal to <math>\operatorname{dom}(L)</math>. We fix one such <math>\mu_0</math>, but its value is not important as it is only a tool.

We may then transform the Fredholm alternative, stated above for compact operators, into a statement about the solvability of the boundary-value problem (*)–(**). The Fredholm alternative, as stated above, asserts:

* For each <math>\lambda \in \mathbf{R}</math>, either <math>\lambda</math> is an eigenvalue of <math>K</math>, or the operator <math>K - \lambda</math> is bijective from <math>X</math> to itself.

Let us explore the two alternatives as they play out for the boundary-value problem. Suppose <math>\lambda \neq 0</math>. Then either

(A)  <math>\lambda</math> is an eigenvalue of <math>K</math> <math>\Leftrightarrow</math> there is a solution <math>h \in \operatorname{dom}(L)</math> of <math>(L + \mu_0)h = \lambda^{-1}h</math> <math>\Leftrightarrow</math> <math>-\mu_0 + \lambda^{-1}</math> is an eigenvalue of <math>L</math>.

(B) The operator <math>K - \lambda : X \to X</math> is a bijection <math>\Leftrightarrow</math> <math>(K - \lambda)(L + \mu_0) = \operatorname{Id} - \lambda(L + \mu_0) : \operatorname{dom}(L) \to X</math> is a bijection <math>\Leftrightarrow</math> <math>L + \mu_0 - \lambda^{-1} : \operatorname{dom}(L) \to X</math> is a bijection.

Replacing <math>-\mu_0 + \lambda^{-1}</math> by <math>\lambda</math>, and treating the case <math>\lambda = -\mu_0</math> separately, this yields the following Fredholm alternative for an elliptic boundary-value problem:

*For each <math>\lambda \in \mathbf{R}</math>, either the homogeneous equation <math>(L - \lambda)u = 0</math> has a nontrivial solution, or the inhomogeneous equation <math>(L - \lambda)u = f</math> possesses a unique solution <math>u \in \operatorname{dom}(L)</math> for each given datum <math>f \in X</math>.

The latter function <math>u</math> solves the boundary-value problem (*)–(**) introduced above. This is the dichotomy that was claimed in (1)–(2) above. By the [[Spectral theory of compact operators|spectral theorem]] for compact operators, one also obtains that the set of <math>\lambda</math> for which the solvability fails is a discrete subset of <math>\mathbf{R}</math> (the eigenvalues of <math>L</math>). The eigenvalues’ associated eigenfunctions can be thought of as "resonances" that block the solvability of the equation.
